A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
methanol was more effective in stimulating uranium reduction than the other electron donors tested.
bioremediating uranium-contaminated sediments requires a holistic approach that takes into account the geochemical environment, the electron donor, and the microbial ecology.
the use of methanol for uranium bioremediation in contaminated sediments is a promising alternative to the use of more traditional electron donors, such as ethanol or acetate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the extent of uranium reduction was not limited by electron donor availability, but by the ability of the microbial community to reduce uranium.

the extent of uranium reduction is dependent upon the electron donor and that the use of methanol as an electron donor for bioremediating uranium-contaminated sites may result in more effective uranium immobilization than other commonly used electron donors.
